hints.title: Use the two diagonals
hints.body: The diagonals of a square bisect each other at right angles. Use the two given opposite vertices to locate the point through which the other diagonal must pass.
hints.recap: A square combines the diagonal properties of a rectangle and a rhombus.
hints.pitfall: The given segment is a diagonal, not one side of the square.
hints.pause: Calculate the midpoint of the two given vertices.

recall.reminder: A square combines the diagonal properties of a rectangle and a rhombus.

hints.title: Build the perpendicular line
hints.body: Find the gradient of the given diagonal. The required line is perpendicular to it and passes through your midpoint, so use the negative reciprocal gradient in a point-gradient equation.
hints.recap: For finite nonzero perpendicular gradients, their product is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
hints.pitfall: Keep the sign when taking the negative reciprocal.
hints.pause: Calculate the new gradient and use the midpoint to obtain the line equation.

recall.reminder: For finite nonzero perpendicular gradients, their product is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline"><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.

solution:
1. Locate the square centre. The diagonals bisect each other, so both pass through the midpoint of A=(0,2) and C=(4,0), which is (2,1).

2. Find the other diagonal gradient. The gradient of AC is (0−2)/(4−0)=−12. The diagonals are perpendicular, so the gradient of BD is 2.

3. Write the line equation. Through (2,1) with gradient 2, it is y−1=2(x−2), hence y=2x−3.

Answer E. Substituting the midpoint verifies that it lies on this line.
knowledgePattern: Find a square diagonal as the perpendicular bisector of the opposite diagonal
